prompt: A property-management firm runs a small worker service named report-mailer on Amazon ECS. It reads from an Amazon SQS standard queue named report-requests, which receives about 300 messages a day, almost all during office hours. The worker loop calls ReceiveMessage again the moment each call returns, and the queue and the calls both leave the wait time at its default of zero.

The monthly bill shows several million ReceiveMessage requests, nearly all of them returning no messages, and the worker occasionally gets an empty response even though messages are waiting. Reports must still go out within a few seconds of a request arriving.
Which change reduces the empty responses and request cost with the least effort?
options: Add a 60-second sleep to the worker loop after every ReceiveMessage call that returns no messages.
Set the queue's ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds to 20 so that each call waits for a message before it returns.
Raise MaxNumberOfMessages to 10 on every ReceiveMessage call so that each request can return more messages.
Set the queue's DelaySeconds to 20 so that the worker's ReceiveMessage calls are spaced 20 seconds apart.
questions.explanation: With a wait time of zero the worker short-polls: each call queries only a sample of SQS servers and returns at once, so an idle queue produces a stream of billable empty responses, and can even miss messages on unsampled servers. Setting ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds to 20, the maximum, turns on long polling for every call that does not override it: SQS queries all servers and holds the request open until a message arrives or 20 seconds pass, so requests drop by orders of magnitude while a new message is still returned immediately. A 60-second sleep cuts requests but can delay a report by a full minute, which breaks the few-seconds requirement. A larger MaxNumberOfMessages helps on a busy queue but does nothing for an empty one, where every call still returns nothing. DelaySeconds makes each new message invisible for 20 seconds after it is sent; it does not space out receive calls, so it adds latency and leaves the empty polls unchanged.

prompt: A fitness-tracking startup exposes an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API named workouts-api in us-east-2, with 14 routes that each integrate with their own AWS Lambda function. Users sign in through an Amazon Cognito user pool named fit-users, and the mobile app sends the user pool access token in the Authorization header. Today every function decodes the token and verifies its signature with a third-party JWT library, and the same 60 lines of verification code are copied into all 14 functions.

The team wants API Gateway to reject missing, forged or expired tokens before any function runs and to hand the token claims to the functions. Which approach meets these requirements with the least custom code?
options: Create a REQUEST Lambda authorizer that downloads the user pool's JSON Web Key Set, verifies each token, and returns a simple response with the claims in its context.
Turn on IAM authorization for every route and have the app exchange its token for identity pool credentials that it uses to sign each request with SigV4.
Attach a usage plan with API keys to the stage, issue each signed-in user an API key, and have the app send that key in the x-api-key header on every request.
Create a JWT authorizer that uses the user pool's issuer URL and the app client ID as its audience, and attach that authorizer to every route of the API.
questions.explanation: A JWT authorizer on an HTTP API is configuration only: API Gateway fetches the signing keys from the user pool's JWKS endpoint, checks the signature, the issuer, the audience (or the client_id claim that Cognito access tokens carry instead), expiry and any route scopes, and then passes the validated claims to the Lambda integration in the request context. A REQUEST Lambda authorizer can do the same job, but it is exactly the custom verification code the team wants to remove, now running as an extra invocation on every request. IAM authorization would force the app to add an identity pool and SigV4 signing, and the functions would see an IAM identity rather than the user pool claims. HTTP APIs do not support usage plans or API keys at all, and an API key only identifies a caller; it never authenticates one.

prompt: A shipping company defines a Lambda function named label-intake in an AWS SAM template. The function reads and writes items in a DynamoDB table named ShipmentsLedger and sends messages to an SQS queue named label-print-queue, both defined in the same template. The function currently has the AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess and AmazonSQSFullAccess managed policies attached, and a security review has flagged both because they grant access to every table and queue in the account.
Which two changes scope the function's permissions to these two resources without the team writing IAM policy statements by hand?
options: Keep AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess and attach a permissions boundary to the function's role that allows DynamoDB actions on the ShipmentsLedger table ARN only.
Replace AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess with the DynamoDBCrudPolicy policy template under Policies, setting its TableName to a reference to ShipmentsLedger.
Set the function's Role property to the shared execution role that the platform team created for all serverless functions in the account.
Replace AmazonSQSFullAccess with a Connectors entry on the function whose destination is label-print-queue and whose permission is Write.
Replace AmazonSQSFullAccess with the AWSLambdaSQSQueueExecutionRole managed policy so that the function holds only the queue permissions it needs.
questions.explanation: SAM policy templates such as DynamoDBCrudPolicy take a placeholder value like TableName and expand into an IAM statement that allows the item-level read and write actions on that table and its indexes only, and a SAM connector embedded on the function, with the queue as its destination and Write as its permission, makes SAM compose a policy that includes sqs:SendMessage on that queue's ARN alone. Neither needs a hand-written statement. A permissions boundary is itself a policy that someone has to write, and it leaves the over-broad managed policy in place as the thing being trimmed. A shared execution role for every function is the opposite of least privilege, because each function inherits the others' access. AWSLambdaSQSQueueExecutionRole grants the receive and delete actions used by an event source mapping that polls a queue, on every queue, and does not grant SendMessage.

prompt: A ticketing startup runs an AWS Lambda function named seat-hold that writes structured JSON log lines with the fields level, errorCode, errorMessage and requestId to the log group /aws/lambda/seat-hold. After a release this morning the error rate tripled. The on-call developer has selected the last six hours as the time range in the CloudWatch Logs Insights console and wants to see which error messages occurred most often, ranked by count, without exporting the logs or creating any new resources.
Which CloudWatch Logs Insights query returns the ten most frequent error messages for that time range?
options: fields @timestamp, errorCode, errorMessage | filter level = 'ERROR' | sort @timestamp desc | limit 10
filter level = 'ERROR' | stats count(*) as occurrences by bin(1h) | sort occurrences desc | limit 10
filter level = 'ERROR' | stats count_distinct(errorMessage) as occurrences by errorCode | sort occurrences desc | limit 10
filter level = 'ERROR' | stats count(*) as occurrences by errorMessage | sort occurrences desc | limit 10
questions.explanation: Grouping the filtered error lines with stats count(*) by errorMessage produces one row per distinct message with its number of occurrences, and sorting that count in descending order with limit 10 leaves exactly the ten most frequent messages; Logs Insights discovers the JSON fields automatically, so no parse step is needed. The query that sorts by @timestamp returns the ten newest error lines, which says nothing about frequency and may show the same message ten times. Grouping by bin(1h) counts errors per hourly bucket, which is a trend over time rather than a ranking of messages. The count_distinct query reports how many different messages each errorCode produced, which ranks error codes by variety and never names a message or says how often it occurred.

prompt: A brokerage publishes account events such as deposits, trades and withdrawals to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue named ledger-events.fifo, and an AWS Lambda function consumes the queue through an event source mapping. Events for any one customer account must be applied in exactly the order they were sent. Every producer currently sets MessageGroupId to the constant value ledger, and during market open the queue backs up by tens of thousands of messages while the function runs with a concurrency of one.
Which change keeps per-account ordering while letting different accounts be processed in parallel?
options: Set MessageGroupId to the customer account ID on every SendMessage call made by the producers.
Set MessageDeduplicationId to the customer account ID on every SendMessage call made by the producers.
Replace the queue with an SQS standard queue and raise the event source mapping batch size to 10.
Keep the constant message group and enable high throughput mode for FIFO queues on ledger-events.fifo.
questions.explanation: SQS FIFO guarantees ordering within a message group, and the Lambda event source mapping processes different message groups concurrently while keeping each group in order, so using the account ID as the group ID gives one ordered lane per account and lets many accounts drain in parallel. Using the account ID as the deduplication ID would make SQS accept but never deliver any further event for that account sent within the five-minute deduplication interval, silently losing deposits and trades. A standard queue offers at-least-once delivery with best-effort ordering, so events for the same account could be applied out of order. High throughput mode raises the queue's transaction quotas, but a single message group is still delivered strictly in order one batch at a time, so the function stays at a concurrency of one.

prompt: A photo-journaling app for iOS and Android stores each user's images in an Amazon S3 bucket named lumen-journal-media. Users sign in through an Amazon Cognito user pool. The product team wants the app to upload and download images directly from S3 without a backend proxy and without shipping any long-lived AWS credentials in the app. Each user's objects live under a prefix of the form private/identity-id/, where identity-id is the user's Cognito identity ID.
Which two actions should the developer take so that each signed-in user can reach only the objects under that user's own prefix?
options: Create an IAM user for each person who signs up, and store that IAM user's access key pair in the device keychain after the person signs in to the app.
Add a bucket policy that allows object actions on private/${aws:username}/* for the IAM role that the mobile app uses when it calls Amazon S3.
Create a Cognito identity pool with the user pool as an identity provider, and have the app exchange its ID token for temporary credentials of the authenticated role.
Attach a policy to the identity pool's authenticated role that allows object actions on private/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}/* in the bucket.
Have the app send the user pool access token in the Authorization header of each S3 request, so that Amazon S3 validates the signed-in user on every call.
questions.explanation: An identity pool turns a user pool sign-in into short-lived AWS credentials for its authenticated role, and the policy variable cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub resolves to the caller's identity ID at request time, so one role policy confines every user to private/identity-id/ without a per-user policy. Together these give direct, credential-free S3 access scoped per user. Creating an IAM user per person puts long-lived keys on every device and hits the IAM user quota long before the app scales. The aws:username variable exists only for IAM users, so it never resolves for a federated role session and the statement matches nothing. Amazon S3 accepts SigV4 signatures, not Cognito JWTs, so sending the access token in the Authorization header is rejected as a malformed authorization.

prompt: A developer at a print-on-demand company is building a Lambda function named thumbnail-maker, defined in an AWS SAM template, that runs when an object is uploaded to an S3 bucket. Docker is installed on the developer's laptop, and the developer wants to step through the handler with an S3 put event for the key uploads/poster-0412.png before anything exists in AWS.
Which approach lets the developer exercise the handler with a realistic event without deploying any resources to AWS?
options: Run sam sync --watch against a development stack so that each save is deployed, then upload test objects to the bucket to trigger the function.
Run sam local start-api and send a POST request that carries the sample object key to the local endpoint that SAM opens on port 3000.
Run sam local generate-event s3 put with the bucket and key, save the output to a file, and pass that file to sam local invoke with the -e option.
Run sam local start-lambda and configure an S3 event notification on a development bucket to deliver upload events to the local endpoint.
questions.explanation: The sam local generate-event command prints a correctly shaped sample payload for a given service and event type, and sam local invoke runs the function once inside a Lambda-like Docker container with that payload passed through -e, so the handler sees a real S3 put event structure and nothing is created in AWS. Running sam sync --watch is useful for fast cloud iteration, but it deploys a stack to an account, which the requirement rules out. The sam local start-api command only serves functions that have Api or HttpApi events in the template, and an S3-triggered function has none, so there is no route to call. The sam local start-lambda command emulates the Lambda Invoke endpoint for SDK and CLI callers, but S3 event notifications cannot be delivered to an endpoint on a laptop.

prompt: An event-ticketing platform emits a TicketPurchased message whenever a sale completes. Three teams consume these messages: one sends email receipts, one runs fraud scoring, and one loads an analytics warehouse. Today the producer sends each message to a single Amazon SQS queue that all three consumers poll, so each purchase reaches only whichever consumer receives it first. The analytics loader is sometimes stopped for several hours during warehouse maintenance and must catch up afterward without missing any purchase.
Which design delivers every message to every consumer so that a fourth consumer can be added later without changing the producer?
options: Keep the single queue and have each consumer receive messages without deleting them, so the other consumers can read them later.
Have the producer call SendMessage three times for each purchase, once to a separate queue owned by each consuming team.
Publish each message to an Amazon SNS standard topic and subscribe a separate SQS queue for each consuming team to the topic.
Publish each message to an Amazon SNS standard topic and subscribe each team's HTTPS endpoint directly to the topic.
questions.explanation: An SNS topic with one SQS queue subscribed per consumer is the fanout pattern: SNS copies every published message into every subscribed queue, and each queue buffers its copy for up to 14 days, so a consumer that is down for hours simply drains its own queue later, and a new consumer needs only a new subscription. Receiving without deleting does not share messages; each one becomes visible again after the visibility timeout, is processed repeatedly by whichever consumer polls first, and stays until retention expires. Sending to three queues from the producer works but hard-codes the consumer list, so adding a fourth team means a producer change. Subscribing HTTPS endpoints directly gives no buffer: SNS retries an unreachable endpoint according to its delivery policy, for at most an hour, and then gives up, so a loader stopped for hours loses messages.

prompt: A payments company runs a service named auth-gateway on Amazon ECS that publishes a custom metric named PendingAuthorizations with the PutMetricData API every 5 seconds, without setting a storage resolution. When a card network stalls, the backlog jumps from about 50 to more than 4,000 for 15 to 25 seconds and then drains, and merchants see timeouts during those bursts. The existing alarm uses the Average statistic over one 60-second period and has never fired during a burst.
Operations needs an alert within 30 seconds of a burst starting and accepts a higher monitoring charge for this one metric.
Which change detects the bursts within 30 seconds of their start?
options: Keep the metric at standard resolution and switch the alarm to the Maximum statistic over a single 60-second evaluation period.
Publish the metric with StorageResolution set to 1 and create a high-resolution alarm on it that uses a 10-second period.
Publish the metric with StorageResolution set to 1 and keep the alarm on the Average statistic over a 60-second period.
Keep the metric at standard resolution and change the period of the existing alarm to 10 seconds so it evaluates more often.
questions.explanation: Setting StorageResolution to 1 makes CloudWatch store the data points at one-second granularity instead of rolling them into one-minute aggregates, and a high-resolution alarm with a 10-second period then evaluates the backlog every 10 seconds, so a burst is caught well inside 30 seconds; the trade-off is that a high-resolution alarm costs more than a standard one, which operations has accepted. Switching a standard-resolution alarm to Maximum would capture the peak value, but the alarm still evaluates one-minute data points, so the alert can arrive more than a minute after the burst began. High-resolution data under a 60-second Average alarm is averaged back into the same minute that diluted the burst before. A 10-second period on a standard-resolution metric finds data only once a minute, so the alarm keeps lapsing into INSUFFICIENT_DATA rather than detecting anything sooner.

prompt: A ticketing platform runs an Amazon API Gateway REST API named seatmap-api that partners call about 900 times per second. A TOKEN Lambda authorizer named partner-token-check validates each opaque partner token by reading a DynamoDB table and calling an internal revocation service, which adds about 180 ms to every request. Each partner reuses the same token for hours, and the IAM policy the authorizer returns already covers every method a partner may call.
The security team accepts that a revoked token may keep working for up to 10 minutes. Which change reduces the authorizer's latency and cost with the least effort?
options: Configure provisioned concurrency on the authorizer function so that every authorization runs in an execution environment that is already initialized.
Enable API Gateway stage caching with a 600-second TTL on every method, so that repeated partner requests are answered without calling the backend integration.
Replace the Lambda authorizer with a Cognito user pool authorizer and migrate every partner to app clients that use the client credentials grant.
Enable authorizer result caching with a TTL of 600 seconds, so API Gateway reuses the returned policy for the same token without invoking the function.
questions.explanation: With authorizer caching on, API Gateway keys the cached policy on the token in the identity source header and skips the authorizer for repeat requests until the TTL expires; the TTL defaults to 300 seconds and can be raised to 3,600, so 600 seconds fits the accepted revocation window. Because the returned policy already covers every method, the cached result is safe to reuse across the API. Provisioned concurrency only removes cold starts: the function, its DynamoDB read and its 180 ms revocation call still run and bill on every request. Stage caching stores integration responses, not authorization decisions, so the authorizer still runs first on each call. Migrating every partner to Cognito client credentials is a large project when one setting solves the problem.

prompt: A fintech team runs a REST API named ledger-api in Amazon API Gateway with two stages, dev and prod. Both stages integrate with one Lambda function named ledger-handler, which has two aliases, dev and prod, that point at different published versions. Today every stage invokes the unqualified function, so the prod stage runs untested code whenever someone updates the function.
Which two steps make each stage invoke its matching alias with a single API definition and no changes to the function code?
options: Deploy the API to each stage with a deployment description that names the alias, so that API Gateway resolves the matching alias when it invokes the function.
Store the alias name in an environment variable on the function and have the handler invoke itself again under the alias that it reads from that variable.
Enable Lambda proxy integration and pass the stage name in a request header so that the Lambda service routes each request to the alias with that name.
Set the integration's function to ledger-handler:${stageVariables.lambdaAlias} and define a lambdaAlias stage variable with the value dev or prod on each stage.
Run lambda add-permission for each alias's qualified ARN so that apigateway.amazonaws.com may invoke it, scoped to the API's source ARN for that method.
questions.explanation: API Gateway substitutes stage variables into the Lambda integration ARN at request time, so ledger-handler:${stageVariables.lambdaAlias} resolves to the dev alias on the dev stage and the prod alias on the prod stage from one deployment. Because the URI is now dynamic, API Gateway does not add the invoke permission itself, and a resource-based permission on the unqualified function does not cover qualified alias ARNs, so each alias needs its own add-permission grant for the API Gateway service principal. A deployment description is free text that API Gateway never reads when it routes a request. Having the handler re-invoke itself under an alias changes the code and doubles every invocation and its cost. The Lambda service does not route an unqualified invocation to an alias based on a header, so a proxy integration header changes nothing.

prompt: A fleet telematics company sends events to an Amazon EventBridge custom event bus named fleet-bus. Each EngineReading event from the source com.haulwise.telemetry carries detail fields named vin, regionCode (values such as EU-DE-03 or US-TX-11) and coolantTempC. A rule currently matches every EngineReading event and targets an AWS Lambda function named overheat-alert, which discards everything except European vehicles whose coolant temperature is above 110. The function is invoked about 40 million times a day, and fewer than 2,000 of those invocations do any work.
Which change limits the invocations to the relevant events with the least operational overhead?
options: Add an input transformer to the rule target that removes events with a coolantTempC of 110 or below before they reach the function.
Create an EventBridge Pipes pipe with fleet-bus as its source and a filter step on regionCode and coolantTempC that invokes the function.
Send the matched events to an SQS queue and add a filter on regionCode and coolantTempC to the function's event source mapping.
Add numeric matching above 110 on detail.coolantTempC and prefix matching on EU- for detail.regionCode to the rule's event pattern.
questions.explanation: EventBridge event patterns support content filtering, so a pattern that combines a numeric comparison on coolantTempC with a prefix match on regionCode makes the rule match only the few thousand relevant events, and the bus never invokes the function for the rest. An input transformer only reshapes the payload delivered to a target after the rule has matched; it cannot drop an event, so every invocation would still happen. EventBridge Pipes reads from sources such as SQS queues, Kinesis and DynamoDB streams, Amazon MQ and Kafka; an event bus can be a pipe target but not a pipe source. Routing through an SQS queue and filtering on the event source mapping would work, but it adds a queue, a mapping and their permissions to do what the rule pattern does on its own.

prompt: A freight-tracking service runs on Amazon EC2 instances in account 111122223333 under an instance role named tracker-app. It must write events to an Amazon Kinesis data stream named shipment-events that the data platform team owns in account 444455556666. That team requires all outside writers to use a role in its account named external-writer, whose trust policy already names the tracker-app role, and tracker-app has been granted sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN.
How should the developer change the application code so it can write to the stream without introducing any long-lived credentials?
options: Call sts:GetSessionToken with the instance role's credentials, and use the returned session credentials to create the Kinesis client for the other account.
Call sts:GetFederationToken with an inline policy that names the stream ARN, and use the returned federated credentials to create the Kinesis client.
Call sts:AssumeRole on the external-writer role ARN, create the Kinesis client from the returned temporary credentials, and refresh them before they expire.
Add the external-writer role to the instance profile beside tracker-app, so that the SDK default credential chain picks up the second role automatically at startup.
questions.explanation: AssumeRole is the STS operation that crosses accounts: the caller's role is trusted by external-writer, so STS returns an access key, secret key and session token that act as external-writer in account 444455556666, and the application builds its Kinesis client from them (or lets an SDK assume-role credential provider refresh them) before the session expires. GetSessionToken must be called with IAM user or root credentials, cannot be called with role credentials, and never changes the account the caller acts in. GetFederationToken is also an IAM-user operation and returns credentials scoped inside the caller's own account. An instance profile holds exactly one role, so a second role cannot be attached beside tracker-app, and the default chain would not assume it anyway.

prompt: A mortgage lender runs a Standard workflow in AWS Step Functions named loan-underwrite. After the automated credit and fraud checks finish, a human underwriter must approve or reject the application in an internal web application, which can take anywhere from ten minutes to three days. The workflow must resume within seconds of the decision and follow a different branch for each outcome.
Which approach pauses the execution until the underwriter decides with the least operational overhead?
options: Add a Task state that invokes an AWS Lambda function synchronously and has the function poll the web application's database for a decision.
Add a waitForTaskToken Task state that hands the task token to the web application, which calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with it.
Add a Wait state that pauses for 259,200 seconds, followed by a Choice state that reads the recorded decision from an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Add a Task state that sends an SQS message with the sync integration pattern so the execution resumes when the web application deletes the message.
questions.explanation: The callback pattern (the .waitForTaskToken suffix on a service integration) pauses a Standard execution, which can run for up to a year, until something calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with the task token, so the approval application returns the decision directly and the workflow resumes immediately on the matching branch. A synchronous Lambda function cannot wait three days, because an invocation stops at the 15-minute maximum timeout, and polling inside it pays for idle compute. A fixed three-day Wait state always waits the full period, so an application approved in ten minutes still sits for three days. The .sync pattern is supported for job-style services such as AWS Batch, Amazon ECS, AWS Glue, AWS CodeBuild and nested Step Functions executions, not for Amazon SQS, so there is no way to wait on a message deletion.

prompt: A courier company exposes a REST API named parcel-tracking through the prod stage of Amazon API Gateway. A new deployment changes the API itself: it adds a request validator, a new body model, and revised mapping templates on the integration. The team wants about 5 percent of real production requests to hit the new deployment while the rest stay on the current one, with the canary's metrics and logs kept separate so they can be compared.
Which approach meets these requirements without creating another stage or giving clients a new URL?
options: Enable canary settings on the prod stage with 5 percent of traffic, deploy the new version to the canary, and promote it once its metrics look healthy.
Create a second stage named prod-v2 and add a weighted Route 53 record that sends 5 percent of DNS lookups to the invoke URL of that new stage.
Configure a weighted alias on the backend Lambda function so that 5 percent of invocations reach the new function version behind the existing prod stage.
Attach a usage plan that throttles the prod stage and redeploy during a quiet window so that only a small share of clients receives the new behavior.
questions.explanation: A REST API stage can carry canary settings: a new deployment goes to the canary, API Gateway routes the configured percentage of requests to it, the canary writes its own CloudWatch metrics and log streams, and promoting it makes it the stage's main deployment while the URL never changes. A second prod-v2 stage is exactly what the team wants to avoid, and both stages share the same execute-api host name, so DNS weighting cannot split traffic between them. A weighted Lambda alias splits only the function code, while this release changes the validator, models and mapping templates that live in API Gateway, so those changes would reach every request or none. A usage plan throttles callers but does not route any share of traffic to a different deployment, and a redeploy changes behavior for every client at once.

prompt: A healthcare scheduling company runs an API named clinic-booking on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. The service is instrumented with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK, and an ADOT Collector sidecar exports spans to AWS X-Ray through the awsxray exporter. Developers set the span attributes clinicId and bookingTier on every request span. The support team now needs to find traces for one clinic with the filter expression annotation.clinicId = "CL-4471", but the search returns nothing, and opening any trace shows clinicId listed under Metadata.
Which change makes the traces searchable by clinicId without changing application code?
options: Replace the ADOT SDK with the AWS X-Ray SDK in the service and call putAnnotation for clinicId inside each request handler.
Search with the filter expression metadata.clinicId = "CL-4471", because the attribute is already being recorded in each trace.
Add clinicId to the indexed_attributes list of the awsxray exporter in the ADOT Collector configuration and redeploy the sidecar.
Raise the X-Ray sampling rule to a fixed rate of 100 percent so that every request carrying a clinicId value is recorded and indexed.
questions.explanation: By default the awsxray exporter translates every OpenTelemetry span attribute into X-Ray metadata, which is stored but not indexed; listing clinicId under indexed_attributes in the collector configuration turns that attribute into an annotation, which filter expressions can search, and only the sidecar configuration changes. Switching to the X-Ray SDK rewrites instrumentation code, and the X-Ray SDKs are in maintenance mode with ADOT as the recommended path. A metadata filter is not possible, because filter expressions only query annotations and built-in fields, never metadata. Sampling every request records more traces, but each one still carries clinicId as metadata, so the search still returns nothing. Setting the aws.xray.annotations span attribute in code would also work, but that is a code change.

prompt: A utility company runs an AWS Lambda function named reading-ingest on nodejs22.x that writes smart-meter readings to an Amazon DynamoDB table named MeterReadings, which uses provisioned capacity with auto scaling. Readings arrive in short bursts at the top of each hour, and during each burst callers see ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors for a few seconds. A previous developer configured the DynamoDBClient from the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 with maxAttempts set to 1 and wrapped each PutItem call in a loop that retries immediately up to five times.
Which change absorbs the bursts with the fewest code changes and without altering the table's capacity settings?
options: Keep the loop but add a fixed one-second pause before every attempt, so that every retry waits the same amount of time.
Switch the writes to the DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) client so that the cache cluster absorbs the burst of PutItem calls.
Increase the function's memory to 3,008 MB so that each attempt in the retry loop completes more quickly.
Remove the custom loop and set retryMode to adaptive with a higher maxAttempts so the SDK backs off with jitter.
questions.explanation: The AWS SDKs already retry throttling errors with exponential backoff and random jitter, which spreads retries out until capacity frees up; the previous configuration disabled that, and the immediate loop retries hardest exactly when the table is saturated. Deleting the loop and restoring SDK retries with a higher maxAttempts fixes it in client configuration alone (adaptive mode also adds client-side rate limiting; standard mode works too). A fixed one-second pause makes every throttled caller retry in lockstep, so the retries collide again a second later. DAX is a write-through cache, so every write still consumes the table's write capacity and is throttled the same way. More memory makes each call marginally faster but adds no write capacity, so the loop simply exhausts its attempts sooner.

prompt: A billing team runs six services on an Amazon ECS cluster that uses EC2 container instances. One service, invoice-render, reads templates from an Amazon S3 bucket named invoice-templates and sends completion messages to an Amazon SQS queue named render-done. Its container image currently includes an env file holding the access key pair of an IAM user, and a security review has flagged those keys.
Which change removes the long-lived keys and limits the S3 and SQS access to invoice-render alone, with the least operational overhead?
options: Create an IAM role that trusts ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com and holds the bucket and queue permissions, set it as the task role, and remove the keys from the image.
Attach the bucket and queue permissions to the container instance role, so that every container on the instance can obtain them from the instance metadata service.
Add the bucket and queue permissions to the task execution role, which the ECS agent hands to the application container so the SDK can call both services.
Store the IAM user's access key pair in Secrets Manager, inject it into the container as secrets in the task definition, and rotate the keys every 90 days.
questions.explanation: A task role is delivered only to the containers of that task through the ECS container credentials endpoint, which the AWS SDK default credential chain reads automatically, so invoice-render gets short-lived credentials and no other service on the same hosts inherits them. Putting the permissions on the container instance role grants them to all six services, and to anything else on the instances that can reach the metadata service. The task execution role is used by the ECS agent itself to pull images, write logs and fetch injected secrets; its credentials are not exposed to application code. Moving the IAM user's keys into Secrets Manager hides them better but leaves long-lived keys in place, plus a rotation job that someone must own.

prompt: A ticketing company keeps an AWS SAM template whose function resources set CodeUri to local folders such as functions/seat-hold/ and whose layer sets ContentUri to layers/shared/. Developers deploy it from their laptops with sam deploy without trouble. A new AWS CodeBuild step in the release pipeline runs aws cloudformation deploy against the same template.yaml, and the deployment fails because CloudFormation cannot use the local folder paths as code locations.
Which change to the build step fixes the deployment with the least change to the template?
options: Add CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND to the aws cloudformation deploy command so that the SAM transform can resolve the local folders while it expands the template.
Zip each function folder and the layer folder in the build, commit the archives beside the template, and point CodeUri and ContentUri at the .zip names.
Rewrite each function to use the InlineCode property so that the template carries the source directly, and remove the CodeUri and ContentUri properties.
Run sam package or aws cloudformation package with an S3 bucket and an output template file first, then deploy the packaged template that it writes.
questions.explanation: The package command zips each local CodeUri and ContentUri folder, uploads the archives to the named S3 bucket, and writes a copy of the template in which those local paths are replaced with S3 locations, which is what CloudFormation needs; sam deploy does the same step implicitly, which is why laptops never hit the error. CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND only acknowledges that the template contains a transform that expands it, and it gives CloudFormation no way to read files on the build host. Committing zip archives still leaves local file names in the template, which CloudFormation cannot open any more than it can open folders. InlineCode suits only small functions without bundled dependencies, it would mean rewriting the function packaging, and a layer has no inline form at all.

prompt: A travel booking site calls a partner airline's seat-map HTTP API from an AWS Lambda function named seatmap-fetch. A few times a week the partner API is unavailable for five to fifteen minutes. During each outage every call waits for the full 10-second client timeout, the function's concurrency climbs past 900, and unrelated functions in the account start to be throttled. The site can show a cached fallback seat map while the partner is down.
Which approach stops the outages from consuming concurrency while resuming partner calls automatically once the API recovers?
options: Add a circuit breaker that tracks failures in a shared DynamoDB item and fails fast during a cooldown before a trial call.
Raise the HTTP client's retry count to five with exponential backoff so that calls made during an outage eventually succeed.
Increase the function's timeout to 15 minutes so that slow partner calls are no longer cut off by the Lambda runtime.
Configure provisioned concurrency on the function so that the slow invocations no longer draw from the account's concurrency pool.
questions.explanation: A circuit breaker turns repeated failures into an open state in which calls are rejected immediately, so the function returns the cached seat map in milliseconds instead of holding an execution environment for ten seconds; after a cooldown it lets a trial request through and closes again once the partner answers. Keeping the state in a shared store such as DynamoDB lets every execution environment see the same breaker. More retries with backoff suit brief throttling, but during a fifteen-minute outage they multiply the time each invocation is stuck and make the concurrency spike worse. A 15-minute timeout lets each stuck call live even longer. Provisioned concurrency is a pre-initialized portion of the account's concurrency, not capacity outside it, and it does nothing to make the calls finish faster.

prompt: A currency exchange startup runs an AWS Lambda function named fx-quote on the python3.13 runtime behind an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Traffic is a steady 40 requests per second, so nearly every invocation lands on an already warm execution environment. Inside the handler, each invocation creates a new boto3 client, opens a new TLS connection to an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster, and downloads a 6 MB file of currency reference data from Amazon S3. The file is replaced once a day, and the business accepts reference data up to one hour old.
The business logic itself takes about 20 ms, yet the median duration is 480 ms. The database has ample connection headroom.
Which two changes reduce the per-invocation latency with the fewest new resources?
options: Create the boto3 client and open the database connection at module level, outside the handler, and reconnect only if the connection has closed.
Configure provisioned concurrency of 10 on an alias so that the client, the connection and the file are prepared before each request arrives.
Raise the function memory to 3,008 MB so that the TLS handshake and the 6 MB download finish faster on every invocation of the function.
Store the currency reference data in an environment variable so that Lambda loads it along with the rest of the function configuration.
Keep the reference file in a global variable or in /tmp with its download time, and fetch it from S3 again only once it is over an hour old.
questions.explanation: Lambda reuses a warm execution environment for later invocations, so anything created at module level during initialization survives between requests: moving the client and the database connection out of the handler removes the TLS handshake from nearly every request, provided the code reconnects when an idle connection has been closed, and caching the reference file in memory or in /tmp with a one-hour refresh removes the S3 download from all but one request per hour. Provisioned concurrency only pre-runs the initialization code, and here all of the slow work sits inside the handler, so it would still run on every request while adding cost. More memory may shave some time off each handshake and download but still repeats them on every invocation. Environment variables are capped at 4 KB in aggregate, far below a 6 MB file.

prompt: A SaaS HR platform keeps every tenant's data in one Amazon DynamoDB table named EmployeeRecords, whose partition key is TenantId. A Lambda function named hr-api authenticates each request, then calls sts:AssumeRole on a role named tenant-scoped-data with a session tag TenantId set to the caller's tenant, and uses those credentials for its DynamoDB calls. The role's trust policy already allows sts:TagSession.
Auditors want IAM itself to guarantee that a bug in a query cannot return another tenant's items. Which permissions policy on tenant-scoped-data enforces this with the least ongoing effort?
options: Allow the item actions on the table with a ForAllValues:StringEquals condition on dynamodb:LeadingKeys that matches ${aws:PrincipalTag/TenantId}.
Allow the item actions on the table with a condition on dynamodb:Attributes that lists only the attribute names each tenant is entitled to read or write.
Allow the item actions on the table and require the function to send a FilterExpression on TenantId with every Query and Scan request it makes.
Create one table for each tenant, and add a policy statement naming that tenant's table ARN to the role whenever a new tenant signs up.
questions.explanation: The dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition key compares the partition key values a request touches with the policy, and the aws:PrincipalTag variable resolves to the session tag at request time, so one static statement lets each session read and write only items whose TenantId equals its own tag; a buggy query for another tenant fails with AccessDenied. A dynamodb:Attributes condition restricts which attribute names may be returned or written, not which items, so it isolates nothing between tenants. IAM cannot require a FilterExpression, and a filter is applied after items are read, so the protection would depend on the same code the auditors distrust. A table per tenant works but adds table sprawl, a policy edit on every sign-up and eventually the role policy size limit.

prompt: A retail team deploys one AWS SAM template for a service named loyalty-points to a staging stack in us-east-2 and a production stack in us-west-2. Each environment needs its own stack name, artifact bucket, and parameter overrides for TableName and LogLevel. Engineers type long sam deploy commands from a wiki page, and last week staging parameter values were deployed to the production stack by mistake.
Which approach deploys the same template to both environments with the least room for operator error?
options: Keep two copies of template.yaml, one for each environment, with that environment's stack settings and parameter values written in as defaults.
Wrap sam deploy in a shell script that exports each parameter override as an environment variable named after the parameter before it calls sam deploy.
Define staging and prod deploy parameter tables in samconfig.toml with each stack name, Region and parameter overrides, then run sam deploy --config-env.
Run sam deploy --guided before every deployment and answer each prompt with the stack name, Region and parameter values for the target environment.
questions.explanation: The SAM CLI reads named environments from samconfig.toml, so tables such as [staging.deploy.parameters] and [prod.deploy.parameters] hold each stack name, Region, bucket and parameter_overrides, and sam deploy --config-env prod applies exactly that set from one template that is checked into source control. Two copies of the template drift apart as soon as someone fixes a resource in only one of them. The SAM CLI does not read parameter overrides from arbitrarily named environment variables, so the wrapper script would pass nothing and the stack would fall back to the template defaults. Running a guided deploy every time reintroduces the manual typing that caused the incident, and by default it writes the answers into the default environment of the config file.

prompt: A shipping company exposes POST /shipments on an Amazon API Gateway REST API with a Lambda integration to a function named shipment-create. Clients regularly send bodies that omit the required destinationPostcode field or send weightKg as a string, and every one of those requests invokes the function only for it to reject the payload. The team wants API Gateway itself to return a 400 response for these bodies before the backend is invoked, without writing validation code.
Which two steps make API Gateway reject the invalid bodies?
options: Create an application/json model whose JSON Schema requires destinationPostcode and declares weightKg as a number.
Add a mapping template to the integration request that strips every property the expected body schema does not define, before the function is invoked.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the stage that blocks any request whose body is larger than 8 KB in size.
Set the method's request validator to one that validates the body, and set the model as the method's request model for application/json.
Attach a REQUEST-type Lambda authorizer that inspects the body and returns a Deny policy when a required field is missing.
questions.explanation: API Gateway REST APIs validate request bodies against a model written in JSON Schema draft 4, but only when the method also has a request validator that validates the body and the model is set as the method's request model for the content type; together they reject a nonconforming body with 400 Bad Request before the integration is called. A mapping template transforms the payload sent to the backend and never rejects a request, so the invalid body would still reach the function. A WAF size rule blocks large requests, not small well-formed ones with a missing field or a wrong type. A REQUEST Lambda authorizer receives headers, query strings, path parameters, stage variables and request context, but not the request body, and it would still be an extra function to write and pay for.

prompt: A retail company exposes an internal Amazon API Gateway REST API named pricing-internal, and every method uses AWS_IAM authorization. A Lambda function named quote-builder in the same account calls GET /prices/{sku} on that API with a plain HTTPS client, and every call returns 403 Forbidden. The function's execution role has no permissions that mention API Gateway.
What should the developer do so that quote-builder can call the API while following least privilege?
options: Grant the execution role execute-api:Invoke on that method's ARN, and sign each request with Signature Version 4 using the role credentials for the execute-api service.
Create an API key, associate it with a usage plan for the stage, and have the function send that key in the x-api-key header of every request to the API.
Grant the execution role apigateway:GET on the API's resources, and send the execution role ARN in the Authorization header of every request that it makes to the API.
Grant the execution role execute-api:Invoke on that method's ARN, and let API Gateway read the caller's role from the Lambda invocation context.
questions.explanation: IAM authorization means API Gateway evaluates the SigV4 signature on the request, identifies the signing principal and checks that it is allowed execute-api:Invoke on the specific method ARN, so the role needs that permission scoped to GET /prices/* and the client must sign with the role's temporary credentials for the execute-api service. An API key is used for usage plans and throttling, not for authentication, and an IAM-authorized method still rejects the unsigned request. The apigateway:GET action governs the management API that reads API definitions, not invoking them, and a role ARN in a header is not a credential. Granting execute-api:Invoke alone is not enough either: API Gateway knows nothing about the caller's role unless the request is signed.

prompt: A fintech start-up serves GET /quote from an Amazon API Gateway REST API that uses a Lambda proxy integration with a python3.13 function named quote-pricing. The handler ends with return {"price": 42.5, "currency": "USD"}. CloudWatch Logs show every invocation completing successfully in about 80 ms, yet clients always receive 502 Bad Gateway, and the API's execution logs report a malformed Lambda proxy response.
Which change makes clients receive the quote with the fewest changes?
options: Raise the function timeout and set the API Gateway integration timeout to 29 seconds so the response is not cut off.
Switch the method to a non-proxy Lambda integration and add integration and method responses that map the result.
Add a Content-Type header of application/json to the method response configuration in API Gateway.
Return a dict with statusCode 200, a headers map, and a body set to json.dumps of the result.
questions.explanation: With a Lambda proxy integration API Gateway passes the function's return value straight through, so it must have the proxy response shape: an integer statusCode, optional headers, and a body that is a string. A bare dictionary has no statusCode and its data is not a string body, so API Gateway reports a malformed proxy response and returns 502; returning statusCode 200 with json.dumps of the result as the body fixes it in one line. The timeouts are irrelevant, because the function finishes in 80 ms and an integration timeout would produce 504, not 502. A non-proxy integration with mapping and method responses would also work, but it is a much larger reconfiguration than a handler change. Method response settings do not reshape a proxy integration's output, so a header defined there leaves the malformed response unchanged.

prompt: A mobile game studio runs its matchmaking service as a Lambda function named match-maker. A new matchmaking algorithm is already in the deployed code behind a boolean check, and the team wants to roll it out gradually over 30 minutes, so that a growing share of the function’s execution environments picks up the new value. If the CloudWatch alarm match-maker-timeouts fires during the rollout, the flag must turn itself back off.
Which approach meets these requirements without publishing new function code or versions?
options: Store the flag in a Lambda environment variable and publish a new function version with weighted alias routing whenever the flag value has to change.
Store the flag in a Parameter Store parameter that the function reads on every invocation, with an EventBridge rule that resets it when the alarm fires.
Create an AWS AppConfig feature flag, deploy it with a linear strategy and the alarm as an environment monitor, and read it through the AppConfig extension.
Store the flag in a DynamoDB item and enable DynamoDB Streams so that a second function reverts the item whenever the alarm changes its state.
questions.explanation: AWS AppConfig deploys a feature flag configuration to an environment using a deployment strategy that controls growth over time, such as a linear rollout over 30 minutes, and it watches the CloudWatch alarms registered as monitors on that environment, rolling the configuration back automatically if one fires during the deployment or bake time. The AppConfig Agent Lambda extension caches the flag locally, so the code reads it without new versions. An environment variable change requires publishing a new version, which the requirement rules out. A Parameter Store value flips for every request at once, so there is no gradual rollout, and the revert logic is custom. A DynamoDB item with a stream-driven reverter is also custom code, adds a read to each invocation, and still offers no gradual exposure.

prompt: A photo-printing service runs an AWS Lambda function named thumb-forge on the python3.13 runtime that resizes uploaded images with the Pillow library. The function is configured with 512 MB of memory, its average duration is 6.2 seconds, and its maximum memory used never exceeds 180 MB. Profiling shows the work is almost entirely CPU-bound and single-threaded. A teammate argues that memory is irrelevant because the function uses barely a third of what it has.
Which change is most likely to cut the duration with little or no increase in cost per invocation?
options: Lower the memory to 256 MB, because the function never uses more than 180 MB and Lambda bills for the memory that is allocated.
Raise the memory toward 1,769 MB and measure with AWS Lambda Power Tuning, because Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory.
Raise the function timeout to 15 minutes and enable provisioned concurrency so that each invocation receives a larger CPU share.
Increase the ephemeral /tmp storage to 10,240 MB so that Pillow can spill its intermediate image buffers to local disk faster.
questions.explanation: Lambda assigns CPU in proportion to configured memory, reaching the equivalent of one full vCPU at 1,769 MB, so a single-threaded CPU-bound function at 512 MB is starved of compute rather than memory; raising memory shortens the duration roughly in step with the added CPU, and because billing is memory multiplied by duration the cost per invocation stays about flat or falls, which Power Tuning confirms with real measurements. Halving the memory to 256 MB also halves the CPU, roughly doubling the duration, so it saves nothing and makes the function slower. A longer timeout only allows a slow invocation to run longer, and provisioned concurrency removes initialization latency without granting more CPU. Larger /tmp storage helps disk-heavy work, not a CPU-bound resize that fits comfortably in memory.

prompt: A telemedicine company stores clinician visit notes as JSON documents of about 2 MB each in Amazon S3. Policy requires the application to encrypt each document with the customer managed AWS KMS key alias/visit-notes before writing it. A developer's first attempt calls the KMS Encrypt operation on the whole document and fails with a ValidationException, because Encrypt accepts at most 4,096 bytes of plaintext.
How should the developer encrypt the documents under the KMS key while keeping the number of KMS requests to a minimum?
options: Split each document into 4 KB chunks, call Encrypt on every chunk with the key, and store the resulting ciphertext chunks together in their original order in S3.
Request a service quota increase for the Encrypt plaintext size so that the key accepts payloads of up to 4 MB, then keep calling Encrypt on each document.
Call GenerateDataKey, encrypt the document locally with the plaintext data key, store the encrypted data key beside the ciphertext, and discard the plaintext key.
Call GenerateRandom once for a 256-bit value, store it in a Lambda environment variable, and use it to encrypt every document locally with AES-GCM.
questions.explanation: Envelope encryption is the pattern KMS is built for: one GenerateDataKey request returns a plaintext data key and the same key encrypted under alias/visit-notes, the application encrypts the 2 MB document locally with AES-GCM, and only the small encrypted data key needs a Decrypt call later. The AWS Encryption SDK packages exactly this flow. Chunking a 2 MB document into 4 KB pieces costs about 500 Encrypt requests per document and quickly runs into KMS request quotas. The 4,096-byte plaintext limit on Encrypt is fixed, not an adjustable quota. A random value stored in an environment variable is a single static key that never touches KMS again, so access to it is neither controlled by the key policy nor logged per use in CloudTrail.

prompt: A market-data firm writes price ticks to an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream named trade-ticks that has 8 shards in provisioned mode. Five independent applications read the full stream, each with its own polling loop that calls GetRecords. Since the fifth application was added, the consumers report ReadProvisionedThroughputExceeded errors and lag of several seconds, while the producers are well within the stream's write limits.
Which change gives each application its own read throughput with the lowest propagation delay?
options: Double the stream to 16 shards with UpdateShardCount so the read throughput that the five applications share is doubled.
Increase the stream's data retention period to seven days so that applications that fall behind can catch up later.
Register each application as an enhanced fan-out consumer and switch it from polling to SubscribeToShard.
Raise the Limit parameter on every GetRecords call to 10,000 records so that each request returns more data per call.
questions.explanation: Shared-throughput consumers split each shard's 2 MB per second of reads and its five GetRecords calls per second, so a fifth poller pushes all of them over the limit. An enhanced fan-out consumer gets its own dedicated 2 MB per second per shard, and records are pushed over HTTP/2 through SubscribeToShard with a typical propagation delay of about 70 ms, independent of the other registered consumers. Resharding to 16 shards raises the shared limits, but every application still competes for them and still pays the polling delay. A longer retention period only lets laggards recover later; it does not stop them from lagging. A larger Limit returns more records per call but cannot exceed the 2 MB per second shard read limit, so bigger reads simply hit it sooner.

prompt: A hotel booking site runs on an AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment named booking-web with six instances behind an Application Load Balancer. During the last release a configuration error broke the new version on half of the instances, and putting the old version back took another full deployment. The team now requires full serving capacity throughout each deployment and wants a failed deployment to leave the original instances untouched.
Which deployment policy meets these requirements while keeping the same environment and URL?
options: Immutable, which launches a full set of new instances in a temporary Auto Scaling group and terminates only those new instances if the deployment fails.
Rolling with additional batch, which launches one extra batch of instances first and then updates the existing instances in batches until all are done.
Rolling, which takes one batch of existing instances out of service at a time, deploys the new version to it, and returns it to the load balancer.
All at once, which deploys the new version to every existing instance in the environment simultaneously and restarts the application server on each.
questions.explanation: An immutable deployment never touches the running instances: Elastic Beanstalk launches a complete set of new instances with the new version in a temporary Auto Scaling group, moves them into the environment only once they pass health checks, and on failure terminates just the new instances, so capacity stays full and rollback is quick and safe. Rolling with additional batch preserves capacity, but it updates the original instances in place, so a failure part-way leaves a mix of versions and recovery is another deployment. Rolling removes a batch from service at a time and therefore reduces capacity, with the same mixed-version failure mode. All at once updates every instance together, causing a brief outage and leaving no healthy original instances if the new version is broken.

prompt: A digital wallet app records peer-to-peer transfers in two Amazon DynamoDB tables in the same account and Region. A transfer must reduce the sender's balance in a table named Wallets, but only if the balance covers the amount, increase the recipient's balance in the same table, and add an item to a table named LedgerEntries. The AWS Lambda function named transfer-post makes these three writes as separate calls.
Twice this month the function timed out after the debit and before the credit, and the sender lost money that the recipient never received.
Which change guarantees that either all three writes take effect or none do, with the least custom code?
options: Combine the three writes into a single BatchWriteItem request so that DynamoDB applies them to both tables together.
Enable DynamoDB Streams on Wallets and have a second function reverse any debit that has no matching credit after a minute.
Read both wallet items with strongly consistent reads before each write, and retry any write that fails until it succeeds.
Send one TransactWriteItems request with Update actions for both wallets, a condition on the sender's balance, and a ledger Put.
questions.explanation: TransactWriteItems groups up to 100 actions across one or more tables in the same account and Region into a single all-or-nothing operation, so the conditional debit, the credit and the ledger Put either all commit or, if the balance condition fails or the request conflicts, all are canceled with a TransactionCanceledException that lists the reason per action. BatchWriteItem is not atomic: some writes can succeed while others come back as UnprocessedItems, and it supports only puts and deletes with no condition expressions, so it cannot even express the conditional debit. A stream-driven compensator leaves balances wrong until it runs. Strongly consistent reads show the latest data but give no atomicity, and retrying from code that has already timed out cannot finish the transfer.

prompt: A genomics lab receives sequencing files in an Amazon S3 bucket named genome-uploads in eu-west-1. The upload scripts run under several IAM roles in the lab's own account, and those roles get their S3 permissions from identity-based policies. An audit found that two older scripts still send requests to the plain HTTP endpoint.
Which bucket configuration makes Amazon S3 reject every request to the bucket that is not sent over TLS, with the least effort?
options: Enable default encryption with SSE-KMS on the bucket so that every object is encrypted under a KMS key before Amazon S3 writes it to storage.
Add a bucket policy statement that denies all S3 actions on the bucket and its objects for every principal when aws:SecureTransport is false.
Add a bucket policy statement that allows s3:PutObject for the upload roles only when aws:SecureTransport is true for the incoming request to the bucket.
Add a bucket policy statement that denies s3:PutObject unless the request includes the x-amz-server-side-encryption header with aws:kms.
questions.explanation: An explicit Deny conditioned on aws:SecureTransport being false overrides any Allow, whether it comes from an identity-based policy or the bucket policy, so every plain HTTP request to the bucket or its objects is refused no matter which role sends it. Default SSE-KMS encryption protects objects at rest and says nothing about how the request traveled. An Allow conditioned on secure transport does not block anything, because the roles in the same account are already allowed by their identity-based policies and an unmet Allow simply does not apply. Requiring the server-side encryption header again concerns encryption at rest; a script can send that header over plain HTTP and the request would still be accepted.

prompt: An online retailer publishes order events to an Amazon SNS standard topic named order-events, about 1.4 million messages per day. Every message carries a message attribute named eventType with one of the values OrderPlaced, OrderShipped, OrderCanceled or RefundIssued. An AWS Lambda function named refund-ledger is subscribed to the topic but only handles RefundIssued events, so it discards about 97 percent of the invocations it receives.
Which change stops the unwanted invocations with the least code and operational overhead?
options: Keep the subscription as it is and add a check at the top of the handler that returns immediately unless eventType is RefundIssued.
Create a second SNS topic for refunds and change the publisher so that it also sends every RefundIssued event to the new topic.
Attach the filter policy {"eventType": ["RefundIssued"]} to the subscription, with the filter policy scope set to MessageAttributes.
Subscribe an Amazon SQS queue to the topic instead and have the function read from the queue with an event source batch size of 10.
questions.explanation: A subscription filter policy is evaluated by SNS before delivery, so with a policy matching eventType RefundIssued on the message attributes, SNS delivers only refund events to refund-ledger and the other 97 percent never invoke the function; it is a configuration change on the subscription with no code involved. An early return in the handler still pays for every invocation and still consumes concurrency, it only makes each wasted call shorter. A dedicated refunds topic works but requires a publisher code change and another topic to operate. Moving the function behind an SQS queue with a batch size of 10 reduces the number of invocations, yet the function still receives and discards every unwanted message, now with a queue to manage as well.

prompt: A lending company serves a REST API named loan-quotes in Amazon API Gateway from a stage named prod in eu-west-1. Twenty minutes ago a pipeline created a new deployment for prod that edited an integration request mapping template, and the template now drops the applicantId path parameter, so every quote request fails. The backend Lambda functions were not changed, and the prod stage's deployment history still lists the deployment that was active before the release.
Which action restores the previous behavior of the prod stage with the fastest recovery and without rebuilding or redeploying anything?
options: Change the prod stage's active deployment back to the previous deployment ID, from its deployment history or with update-stage on /deploymentId.
Revert the commit in the Git repository and let the pipeline rebuild the project and run its full deployment to the prod stage once again.
Delete the prod stage and create it again from the previous deployment, then reapply its stage variables, throttling and logging settings.
Re-import the OpenAPI file from the previous release in overwrite mode and create a new deployment of that imported definition to prod.
questions.explanation: A REST API deployment is a snapshot of the API's methods, integrations and mapping templates, and a stage simply points at one, so changing the stage's active deployment from its Deployment history tab, or running update-stage with a replace patch on /deploymentId, puts the earlier snapshot back in service immediately without rebuilding anything. Reverting the commit and letting the pipeline run is a sound long-term fix, but it waits for a full build and deployment while every quote request keeps failing. Deleting and recreating the stage takes the prod URL offline until the new stage exists and discards its stage settings, which must be rebuilt by hand. Re-importing an older OpenAPI file overwrites the current API definition and still needs a new deployment, which is slower and may restore a file that never matched what was live.

prompt: A grocery chain streams point-of-sale records into an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream named pos-sales with 12 shards. An AWS Lambda function named sales-enrich reads it through an event source mapping with a batch size of 500 and the default error-handling settings. Yesterday a single malformed record made the handler throw on every attempt; the IteratorAge metric for that shard climbed for hours while the other 11 shards stayed current.

The team wants the valid records in a failing batch to be processed, a bad record to be retried only a bounded number of times, and the shard ID and sequence numbers of any discarded records kept for investigation, without changing the function code.
Which event source mapping configuration meets these requirements?
options: Configure an SQS dead-letter queue in the function's asynchronous invocation settings so that failed records are moved off the stream.
Raise the ParallelizationFactor to 10 so that each shard is processed by several concurrent batches while the bad record is retried.
Set MaximumRetryAttempts to 0 so that a failing batch is skipped after its first error and the shard moves on to the next batch.
Turn on BisectBatchOnFunctionError, set MaximumRetryAttempts to 3, and add an on-failure destination that sends to an SQS queue.
questions.explanation: By default a stream event source mapping retries a failing batch until the records expire, so one poison record holds its shard in place. BisectBatchOnFunctionError splits a failed batch in half repeatedly, so the valid halves succeed and the bad record ends up isolated; MaximumRetryAttempts (or MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds) bounds the retries, after which Lambda discards the record and moves on, and the on-failure destination receives the shard ID, sequence-number range and error context for the discarded batch (metadata only for an SQS destination). A function-level dead-letter queue applies only to asynchronous invocations, and an event source mapping invokes the function synchronously, so nothing would reach it. A higher ParallelizationFactor adds concurrency per shard, but the bad record is still retried indefinitely. Zero retries skips the whole batch of 500 on its first error, discarding the valid records with it and leaving no record of what was lost.

prompt: A legal-technology firm ships a desktop application named brief-vault that uploads case files of 1 MB to 50 MB to Amazon S3. A client contract requires every file to be encrypted on the user's workstation before it leaves the machine, so that neither the network path nor Amazon S3 ever handles plaintext, and the encryption keys must be protected by a KMS key that the firm controls. The developers do not want to write or maintain their own cryptographic code.
Which approach meets the contract with the least custom cryptographic code?
options: Upload the files over HTTPS to a bucket whose default encryption uses SSE-KMS with the firm's customer managed key, so that S3 encrypts each object.
Upload the files to a bucket that uses dual-layer server-side encryption (DSSE-KMS) with the firm's customer managed key for every object.
Encrypt each file in the application with the AWS Encryption SDK and a KMS keyring for the firm's key, then upload the encrypted message to S3.
Call the KMS Encrypt operation on each file from the application with the firm's key, and upload the ciphertext blob that KMS returns to S3.
questions.explanation: The AWS Encryption SDK performs client-side envelope encryption for the application: the KMS keyring obtains a data key under the firm's KMS key, the SDK encrypts the file locally and emits a portable encrypted message that carries the encrypted data key, so only ciphertext ever leaves the workstation and no hand-written cryptography is involved. SSE-KMS encrypts at rest inside Amazon S3, which means S3 receives the plaintext (protected only by TLS in transit), breaking the contract. DSSE-KMS adds a second server-side layer but has the same flaw: the encryption still happens in S3 after the plaintext arrives. Calling KMS Encrypt directly fails for these files, because that operation accepts at most 4,096 bytes of plaintext.

prompt: A travel publisher serves its mobile app content through an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of an Application Load Balancer. The origin returns English, German or Japanese JSON based on the Accept-Language request header, and the app always sends exactly one of the values en, de or ja. The cache behavior uses the managed CachingOptimized cache policy together with the managed AllViewer origin request policy. Users in Munich report that they sometimes receive Japanese content.
Which change makes CloudFront keep a separate cached copy for each language while still serving cached responses from the edge?
options: Create a custom origin request policy that forwards Accept-Language so the header reaches the load balancer on every cache miss.
Attach a custom cache policy that includes the Accept-Language header in the cache key while keeping the current TTL settings.
Set the default, minimum and maximum TTLs in the cache policy to 0 seconds so that CloudFront sends every request to the origin.
Configure the load balancer targets to add a Vary: Accept-Language response header so that CloudFront stores one copy per language.
questions.explanation: Only values in the cache key make CloudFront store separate objects, and a cache policy that includes Accept-Language yields one cached copy per header value, three here; headers in a cache policy are also forwarded to the origin automatically, so the origin still sees the language. A custom origin request policy only controls what reaches the origin on a miss, which AllViewer already does, and values it adds are never part of the cache key, so the first language cached keeps being served to everyone. Zero TTLs stop the wrong copy from being served by disabling caching, which defeats the requirement to serve from the edge. CloudFront does not split its cache on a Vary response header, apart from its own handling of Accept-Encoding, so Vary changes nothing.

prompt: A warehouse platform uses AWS CodeDeploy in-place deployments to update a worker named inventory-sync on a fleet of EC2 instances. The worker consumes queue messages, has no load balancer, and exposes a health endpoint on localhost:8081 once it has started. A recent revision installed cleanly but crashed on startup, and the deployment was still reported as successful.
Which change makes CodeDeploy fail the deployment on any instance where the worker does not become healthy after it starts?
options: Add a BeforeInstall hook to appspec.yml that runs a script which polls localhost:8081/health and exits with a nonzero code when the check fails.
Add an ApplicationStop hook to appspec.yml that runs a script which polls localhost:8081/health and exits with a nonzero code when the check fails.
Add a post_build command to the CodeBuild buildspec that starts the worker inside the build container and fails the build when the health check fails.
Add a ValidateService hook to appspec.yml that runs a script which polls localhost:8081/health and exits with a nonzero code when the check fails.
questions.explanation: ValidateService is the last lifecycle event of an EC2 in-place deployment, running after ApplicationStart, so a script there sees the newly started worker, and a nonzero exit code or a timeout fails the deployment for that instance, which can trigger an automatic rollback if the deployment group enables one. BeforeInstall runs before the new revision is copied into place and before the worker has started, so the check would test the old process or nothing. ApplicationStop runs first and uses the scripts from the previously deployed revision, so a new check would not take effect until the next deployment and would still run before the new code starts. A post_build check in CodeBuild tests the artifact in a build container, not the real start-up on each instance, so environment-specific crashes would still slip through.

prompt: A payroll provider's AWS Lambda function named payout-post consumes an Amazon SQS standard queue through an event source mapping with a batch size of 10. When a single message in a batch fails validation, for example because of an unknown bank code, the handler raises an exception and all ten messages return to the queue. The nine valid payouts are then processed again, which triggers duplicate-request rejections from the payment processor and floods the logs.
Which two changes make only the failed messages return to the queue while keeping the batch size of 10?
options: Reduce the event source mapping's batch size to 1 so that each failing message is retried on its own.
Add ReportBatchItemFailures to the FunctionResponseTypes setting of the event source mapping for the queue.
Set the maxReceiveCount of the queue's redrive policy to 1 so that a failed batch moves to the dead-letter queue.
Configure an on-failure destination on the event source mapping that sends failed batches to a second SQS queue.
Return batchItemFailures with the itemIdentifier of each failed message instead of raising an exception.
questions.explanation: Partial batch responses need both halves: the event source mapping must list ReportBatchItemFailures in FunctionResponseTypes, and the handler must return a batchItemFailures array with the messageId of each failed record as its itemIdentifier. Lambda then deletes the successful messages and only the listed ones become visible again; if the handler raises an exception instead, the whole batch is still treated as failed. A batch size of 1 isolates failures but abandons the batch size the scenario requires and multiplies invocations tenfold. A maxReceiveCount of 1 sends the entire failed batch, valid payouts included, to the dead-letter queue on the next receive. On-failure destinations on event source mappings apply to stream and Kafka sources; for an SQS source, failed messages are handled by the queue's own redrive policy.
