prompt: A contract-management SaaS provider encrypts every tenant's documents with envelope encryption under one customer managed AWS KMS key, alias/contracts-data. Each tenant's ingestion pipeline runs under its own IAM role, and every one of those roles carries an IAM tag named tenantId whose value is the tenant's ID. A recent incident in staging showed that a misrouted job running under the role for tenant t-2207 could successfully decrypt a data key that had been generated for tenant t-1184.
The security team wants KMS itself to refuse such a cross-tenant decryption and wants each KMS call in AWS CloudTrail to show which tenant it served. Which two actions meet these requirements?
options: Pass an encryption context of tenantId set to the tenant's ID on every GenerateDataKey call, and pass the identical encryption context on every Decrypt call for that tenant.
Create a separate alias for each tenant that points to the shared key, because KMS binds every ciphertext to the alias that was named in the request that originally created it.
Add a key policy condition that allows GenerateDataKey and Decrypt only when kms:EncryptionContext:tenantId equals ${aws:PrincipalTag/tenantId} for the calling role.
Add a key policy condition with ForAllValues:StringEquals on kms:EncryptionContextKeys that lists tenantId as the only encryption context key each role may send.
Store the tenant ID in an S3 object tag beside each encrypted document, and have the pipeline compare that tag with its own tenant before it calls Decrypt.
questions.explanation: An encryption context is authenticated additional data: KMS binds it to the ciphertext, Decrypt succeeds only when the identical, case-sensitive context is supplied, and the context appears in plaintext in the CloudTrail record of each call. Adding a key policy condition that ties kms:EncryptionContext:tenantId to the caller's own tenantId tag then stops a role from even asking for another tenant's context, so a misrouted job fails inside KMS, provided no IAM policy on the tenant roles grants kms:Decrypt on the key without the same condition. Aliases are only friendly names; ciphertext is bound to the key, not to the alias used. A ForAllValues test on kms:EncryptionContextKeys checks key names, not values, and also matches requests that carry no context at all, so t-2207 could still send tenantId t-1184. Comparing an S3 tag in application code is the same kind of check the misrouted job already bypassed; KMS would never enforce it.

prompt: A freight-forwarding company maintains an AWS SAM application with 34 Python functions on python3.13. Every function's .zip package bundles the same internal rates-common library along with pydantic and requests, which makes each package about 18 MB and means that a fix to rates-common requires rebuilding and uploading all 34 packages. The team wants to keep .zip deployment packages and keep the functions out of a VPC.
Which approach removes the duplicated dependencies with the least operational overhead?
options: Upload the shared libraries to an Amazon S3 bucket and download them into /tmp from each function's initialization code.
Publish the shared libraries as a Lambda layer under a python directory and add the layer to each function.
Store the shared libraries on an Amazon EFS file system and mount the file system on every function at /mnt/libs.
Move the shared libraries into a Git submodule that is copied into each function's source folder at build time.
questions.explanation: A Lambda layer is a .zip archive that Lambda extracts into /opt, and for Python the contents of its python directory are added to the import path, so the shared libraries are published once and each function references a layer version instead of bundling its own copy. Layer versions are immutable, so a rates-common fix becomes one new layer version, which SAM can roll out to all 34 functions through a single shared resource reference. Downloading from S3 into /tmp needs custom loader code and adds the download to every cold start. EFS mounts require the functions to be attached to a VPC, which the team ruled out, and they add a file system to manage. A Git submodule removes duplication from the source tree only; every package still bundles its own 18 MB copy and must be rebuilt for each fix.

prompt: A legal technology company is moving a document classifier named pdf-ocr to AWS Lambda on the python3.13 runtime. Its OCR libraries, native dependencies and model files add up to about 2.1 GB unzipped, and an attempt to deploy it as a .zip archive with layers was rejected for exceeding the size limit.
Which approach lets the function run on Lambda while keeping every dependency packaged in the function's deployment artifact?
options: Split the dependencies across five Lambda layers so that each layer archive stays below 50 MB zipped and attach all five layers to the function.
Upload the .zip archive to an S3 bucket and create the function from the S3 object, which raises the unzipped package limit to 10 GB.
Build a container image from the AWS Lambda base image for Python 3.13, push it to Amazon ECR, and create the function from that image.
Download the libraries and model files from S3 into /tmp during initialization after raising the function's ephemeral storage to 10,240 MB.
questions.explanation: A Lambda function packaged as a container image can be up to 10 GB uncompressed, so building from the AWS base image for Python 3.13, pushing it to Amazon ECR and creating the function from the image keeps all 2.1 GB of dependencies inside the deployment artifact. Splitting dependencies across layers does not help, because the 250 MB unzipped limit applies to the function code and all of its layers combined. Uploading the archive through S3 only lifts the 50 MB direct-upload limit on the zipped file, and the 250 MB unzipped limit still applies. Downloading into /tmp at initialization can be made to work, but it moves the dependencies out of the deployment artifact, which the requirement rules out, and adds a large download to every cold start.

prompt: A payments team uses a symmetric customer managed AWS KMS key with KMS-generated key material, aliased alias/ledger-data, to protect ledger records through envelope encryption. Several years of encrypted records are stored, and the application configuration refers to the key by its ARN. A new internal standard requires the key material to be rotated every 180 days.
Which approach meets the standard without re-encrypting existing records or changing the application, with the least operational overhead?
options: Create a new KMS key every 180 days, repoint the alias to it, and run a batch job that re-encrypts every stored record under the newly created key.
Schedule a Lambda function every 180 days that calls RotateKeyOnDemand on the key, because automatic rotation only runs on a fixed yearly schedule.
Enable automatic rotation with a 180-day period, then re-encrypt the existing records, because KMS deletes the old key material after each rotation.
Enable automatic rotation with a 180-day rotation period; KMS keeps all earlier key material and uses it to decrypt older ciphertext automatically.
questions.explanation: Automatic rotation for a customer managed key accepts a custom rotation period between 90 and 2,560 days (365 by default), so a 180-day period meets the standard with one setting; the key ID and ARN never change, and KMS retains every previous version of the key material so data keys encrypted years ago still decrypt without any change. Creating a new key and re-encrypting the archive every 180 days is a recurring project, and the ARN-based configuration would still point at the old key. A scheduled on-demand rotation would work, but it rests on the outdated idea that automatic rotation is fixed at one year and adds a function to maintain. KMS never deletes earlier key material on rotation, so re-encrypting the records is unnecessary work.

prompt: A mobile gaming studio stores player profiles in an Amazon DynamoDB table named PlayerProfiles. A Java service built on the AWS SDK issues about 45,000 eventually consistent GetItem requests per second against a small set of hot keys, while writes stay below 300 per second. Reads already complete in single-digit milliseconds, but a new matchmaking feature needs profile lookups to return in microseconds.
Which solution delivers microsecond read latency with the fewest code changes?
options: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so that DynamoDB scales its read throughput automatically to follow demand.
Create a DynamoDB Accelerator cluster and replace the DynamoDB client with the DAX client, keeping the existing GetItem calls.
Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster and implement cache-aside reads with explicit invalidation on every write in the service.
Add a global table replica in the Region closest to most players and point the read path of the service at that replica.
questions.explanation: DAX is an in-memory, write-through cache built for DynamoDB that serves eventually consistent reads from cache in microseconds, and its client is API-compatible with the DynamoDB client, so the service swaps the client and keeps its GetItem calls unchanged. On-demand capacity mode changes how throughput is provisioned and billed, but every read still goes to DynamoDB at millisecond latency. ElastiCache can also return cached data in microseconds, but the team would have to write cache-aside logic, choose keys and TTLs, and invalidate entries on every write, which is far more code. A global table replica only moves the data closer to some players; reads against it are still DynamoDB reads measured in milliseconds.

prompt: A retailer's AWS Lambda function named catalog-import is invoked asynchronously by Amazon S3 whenever a supplier uploads a CSV file, and it writes the rows into a self-managed PostgreSQL database on Amazon EC2 that allows at most 120 connections. Each invocation opens one connection. At 02:00 a large supplier uploads about 3,000 files at once; the function scales to several hundred concurrent executions, the database refuses connections, and other applications that share it fail. Imports may finish up to an hour later without any business impact.
Which change protects the database with the least operational overhead?
options: Set reserved concurrency of 40 on the function so that excess events are throttled and retried later by Lambda.
Configure provisioned concurrency of 40 on an alias of the function and point the S3 notification at that alias.
Place an Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the database and change the function to connect through the proxy endpoint.
Request a lower Regional concurrent executions quota of 40 for the account through Service Quotas.
questions.explanation: Reserved concurrency is both a guarantee and a ceiling, so at 40 the function can never hold more than 40 database connections. Because S3 invokes the function asynchronously, events that arrive while it is at its limit are throttled and kept in Lambda's internal queue, which retries them for up to the six-hour default maximum event age, so the backlog simply drains over the following minutes. Provisioned concurrency only keeps execution environments initialized; it is not a cap, and the function scales past it on demand. RDS Proxy pools connections only for Amazon RDS and Aurora databases, not for PostgreSQL that runs on EC2. Service Quotas takes requests to raise the account-level concurrency quota, not to lower it, and an account-wide limit would throttle every function in the account rather than this one.

prompt: A developer at a mapping startup builds a Lambda function named tile-index on the python3.13 runtime with the x86_64 architecture. One of its dependencies has no prebuilt Linux wheel for the pinned version, so pip compiles its C extension during installation. The developer works on a Windows laptop with Docker Desktop installed, runs sam build and sam deploy, and every invocation then fails with an import error for the compiled module.
Which change produces a working deployment package without changing the laptop's operating system or setting up a separate build server?
options: Run sam build with --use-container so that the dependencies are installed and compiled inside a Lambda build image for python3.13.
Move the compiled dependency into a Lambda layer that is built on the laptop, attach the layer to the function, and deploy the function again.
Change the function's architecture to arm64 so that Lambda can load compiled modules regardless of the platform that the module was built on.
Deploy with sam sync --code so that only the handler code is uploaded and the Lambda service installs the dependencies from requirements.txt.
questions.explanation: With --use-container, sam build runs the dependency installation inside a container image that behaves like the Lambda environment for the function's runtime and architecture, so the C extension is compiled for Amazon Linux on x86_64 and imports correctly once deployed; Docker Desktop on the laptop is all it needs. Building a layer on the same laptop moves the Windows-compiled module into another archive without changing what it was compiled for. Switching to arm64 makes the mismatch worse, because Lambda loads native code only when it matches both the operating system and the processor architecture. Lambda never installs packages from requirements.txt at deploy or run time, so uploading only the handler code with sam sync --code leaves the module missing entirely.

prompt: A recruitment platform lets job candidates upload video introductions of up to 300 MB from a browser into an Amazon S3 bucket named candidate-media. Candidates have no account; each one receives an emailed application link that a Lambda function named upload-ticket, behind Amazon API Gateway, already validates. The bucket must stay private, the browser must never hold AWS credentials, and each upload must be allowed for only one object key and for no more than 15 minutes.
Which approach lets the browser upload the video with the least development effort?
options: Have upload-ticket use the SDK to create a presigned PUT URL for a single object key that expires in 15 minutes, and have the browser PUT the file straight to that URL.
Have upload-ticket create a presigned PUT URL that expires in 7 days so that a candidate can retry the upload later, and sign it with the function execution role credentials.
Send the video through an API Gateway REST API that uses an S3 service integration to write the request body to the bucket under the candidate's object key.
Add a bucket policy that allows s3:PutObject for all principals on the uploads/ prefix, and have the browser send an unsigned PUT request for the candidate's key.
questions.explanation: A presigned URL carries a signature made with the backend's credentials for one operation on one key, so the browser can PUT that single object directly to Amazon S3 for the 15 minutes requested without ever holding credentials; the bucket only needs a CORS rule allowing PUT from the site's origin. A 7-day expiry breaks the 15-minute requirement, and it would not hold anyway: a URL signed with temporary credentials such as a Lambda execution role's stops working when those credentials expire, whatever expiry was requested, and only IAM user credentials reach the 7-day maximum. Routing the video through API Gateway fails because its request payload limit is 10 MB, far below 300 MB. A bucket policy that allows anonymous PutObject makes the prefix publicly writable, which no time or key limit can repair.

prompt: A streaming video service records player events in an Amazon DynamoDB table named PlaybackEvents that uses on-demand capacity. The partition key is eventDate, a string such as 2026-10-03, and the sort key is eventTime. The application reads events by viewing session, and daily reporting runs from a nightly export. At about 1,500 writes per second the table starts returning throttling errors, and CloudWatch Contributor Insights shows nearly all traffic going to the current day's key.
Which design change removes the throttling while still supporting the session-based reads?
options: Switch the table from on-demand to provisioned mode and set a write capacity well above 1,500 units per second.
Make a high-cardinality attribute such as sessionId the partition key, with eventTime as sort key, in a new table.
Add a global secondary index that uses sessionId as its partition key and keep eventDate as the table's partition key.
Place a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table so that the cluster absorbs the burst of writes.
questions.explanation: A single partition key value is served by one partition, which supports up to 1,000 write units per second, so putting all of a day's writes under one eventDate value creates a hot partition no matter how much table capacity exists. Keying on sessionId spreads writes across many partitions and matches the session-based read pattern; because a table's partition key cannot be changed, that means a new table and a migration. Provisioned mode raises table capacity but not the per-partition limit, so the hot key still throttles. A global secondary index adds a second write for every item and leaves the base table's hot key exactly where it was. DAX is a write-through cache, so every write still lands on the same hot partition.

prompt: A media streaming company runs 14 AWS CodeDeploy deployment groups across five applications in us-west-2, deploying to both AWS Lambda and Amazon ECS. Product teams add new deployment groups every month through their own AWS CloudFormation stacks. The release managers want an email whenever any deployment in the account succeeds or fails, including deployments in groups that do not exist yet, without anyone having to edit each deployment group.
Which approach meets the requirement with the least ongoing maintenance?
options: Add a trigger to every deployment group that publishes DeploymentSuccess and DeploymentFailure events to an Amazon SNS topic.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for CodeDeploy deployment state-change events in the SUCCESS or FAILURE state, targeting SNS.
Create an AWS CloudTrail metric filter on CreateDeployment API calls with a CloudWatch alarm that notifies an Amazon SNS topic.
Schedule a Lambda function every five minutes that calls ListDeployments and GetDeployment and publishes outcomes to SNS.
questions.explanation: CodeDeploy emits a CodeDeploy Deployment State-change Notification event to EventBridge for every deployment, so one rule matching the SUCCESS and FAILURE states for any application and any deployment group, with an SNS topic and email subscriptions as its target, covers all 14 groups and every group created later with no further work. Deployment group triggers do send these events to SNS, but they are configured per group, so every new group needs its own trigger and a forgotten one goes silent. A metric filter on CreateDeployment only sees the API call that starts a deployment, never whether it succeeded or failed. A polling function is custom code to write and maintain, and it reports outcomes up to five minutes late.

prompt: A design agency hosts a React storefront on AWS Amplify Hosting, connected to a private GitHub repository through the Amplify GitHub App, with the main branch deployed as production. Reviewers want every pull request against main built and served at its own address so that QA can test it before merging, and they do not want stale test sites left behind after a pull request is merged or closed.
Which approach meets these requirements with the least ongoing effort?
options: Connect each feature branch to the app in the Amplify console as a new branch deployment, and disconnect the branch by hand after its pull request merges.
Turn on pull request previews for main, so that Amplify builds each pull request to its own preview URL and deletes it once the request closes.
Create a separate Amplify app for each developer that connects to the same repository, and have each developer push feature work to that app's branch.
Add an AWS CodeBuild project that builds each pull request and copies the output to its own S3 prefix behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution.
questions.explanation: Amplify Hosting web previews deploy every pull request made against an enabled branch to a unique preview URL, separate from the production URL, and delete that preview, along with any temporary backend environment created for it, when the pull request is closed; each open pull request counts toward the app's branch quota, which closing it releases. Connecting branches manually does give each one a site, but someone has to add and remove every branch, which is exactly the upkeep and the stale sites the reviewers want to avoid. A separate app per developer multiplies build settings, environment variables and domains, and still gives no per-pull-request environment. A custom CodeBuild and CloudFront pipeline reimplements previews by hand and needs its own trigger, routing and cleanup logic.

prompt: A help-desk product stores tickets in an Amazon DynamoDB table named Tickets, with ticketId as its only key, holding about 60 million items in production. A new dashboard must list all tickets assigned to one agent, newest first, using assigneeId and updatedAt. The current implementation runs a Scan with a filter on assigneeId, which takes minutes and consumes most of the table's read capacity.
Which change supports the new access pattern efficiently without recreating the table?
options: Add a local secondary index with assigneeId as its partition key and updatedAt as its sort key by calling UpdateTable on Tickets.
Add a global secondary index with assigneeId as its partition key and updatedAt as its sort key by calling UpdateTable.
Keep the Scan but run it as a parallel scan with eight segments and a FilterExpression on assigneeId.
Keep the Scan but add a ProjectionExpression so that it reads only the assigneeId and updatedAt attributes.
questions.explanation: A global secondary index can be added to an existing table at any time; DynamoDB backfills it from the current items, and the dashboard can then Query by assigneeId with ScanIndexForward set to false to return the newest tickets first. A local secondary index must share the table's partition key, so it could not be keyed on assigneeId, and local secondary indexes can only be defined when the table is created. A parallel scan finishes sooner but still reads all 60 million items and consumes even more read capacity per second. A ProjectionExpression trims what is returned, not what is read, because read capacity is charged on the full size of every item scanned before any projection or filter is applied.

prompt: A B2B analytics company authenticates users with an Amazon Cognito user pool on the Essentials feature plan. Each user belongs to an organization, and the organization's subscription plan (free, team or enterprise) lives in an Amazon DynamoDB table named OrgAccounts, where the billing system updates it when a customer upgrades. The company's API validates Cognito access tokens and must authorize premium routes on org_id and plan claims in the access token itself, without a database lookup on every request.
Which approach adds current org_id and plan claims to the access tokens with the least custom code?
options: Add a post authentication trigger that reads OrgAccounts and writes org_id and plan into custom user attributes, so that they appear in the tokens after every sign-in.
Add a pre token generation trigger that uses the V1_0 event, reads OrgAccounts, and returns org_id and plan in claimsToAddOrOverride for the access token.
Add a pre token generation trigger that uses the V2_0 event, reads OrgAccounts, and returns org_id and plan as claims under accessTokenGeneration in its response.
Create a user pool group for every organization and every plan, keep memberships in sync with billing, and have the API read both values from cognito:groups.
questions.explanation: The pre token generation trigger runs each time Cognito issues tokens, including on refresh, and the V2_0 event (available on the Essentials and Plus plans) lets the function add claims to the access token through accessTokenGeneration.claimsToAddOrOverride, so a single DynamoDB read at issuance puts current org_id and plan values where the API can authorize on them. A V1_0 event customizes only the ID token, apart from group overrides, so its claimsToAddOrOverride never reaches the access token the API validates. Custom user attributes written by a post authentication trigger appear in the ID token, not the access token, and copying billing data into the directory on every sign-in adds writes and staleness. Encoding organizations and plans as groups means thousands of groups and a sync job for every membership and plan change.

prompt: A warehouse-management service runs as several Amazon ECS tasks that update stock levels in an Amazon DynamoDB table named StockLevels. To record a pick, a task calls GetItem, applies business rules in code that compute the new quantity and reservation fields, and calls PutItem with the result. During peak hours two tasks sometimes process picks for the same SKU at once, and one task's PutItem silently overwrites the other's, so stock counts drift.
Which change detects conflicting writes so they can be retried, while keeping the read-modify-write logic in code?
options: Set ConsistentRead to true on every GetItem call so that each task always reads the most recently written version of the item.
Read the item with TransactGetItems and then write it with TransactWriteItems so that the two steps run inside a transaction.
Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table and have an AWS Lambda function reconcile conflicting versions after they are written.
Add a version attribute and make each PutItem conditional on it matching the value read, incrementing it in the same write.
questions.explanation: Optimistic locking makes each write conditional on the item being unchanged since it was read: the PutItem carries a ConditionExpression that the version attribute still equals the value read and sets it one higher, so a concurrent writer gets a ConditionalCheckFailedException, rereads the item and reapplies its rules instead of overwriting. Strongly consistent reads return the latest committed item at read time, but another task can still write between that read and the PutItem. TransactGetItems and TransactWriteItems are separate calls, and no transaction spans them; an unconditional write inside TransactWriteItems overwrites just as PutItem does. A stream-driven reconciler repairs drift only after the lost update has happened, other tasks read the wrong count in the meantime, and it would have to re-derive the business rules from old and new images.

prompt: A food delivery company builds a container image for a service named orders-svc in AWS CodeBuild and pushes it to Amazon ECR with the tag release-candidate. An integration test stage then runs the image on a test Amazon ECS service, and a later stage deploys release-candidate to production. Last week a second build pushed a new release-candidate between the tests and the deployment, so production ran an image that had never been tested.
Which change guarantees that production runs the exact image that passed the integration tests?
options: Add an ECR lifecycle policy that expires untagged images after one day so that only the most recent release-candidate image remains in the repository.
Configure ECR replication to a second repository that only production uses, so that production deployments pull from a copy of the tested image.
Enable tag immutability, tag each build with its commit ID, and pass the image digest from the build to the test and production task definitions.
Set force new deployment on the production ECS service so that its tasks always pull the newest release-candidate image when the deployment stage runs.
questions.explanation: A digest is a content hash that identifies one image and can never point at anything else, and tag immutability stops a later push from overwriting an existing tag, so tagging by commit ID and passing the digest through the pipeline makes the test stage and the production stage reference the same bytes. An untagged-image lifecycle policy only cleans up old images; it does nothing to stop release-candidate being moved to a new image. Replication copies whatever is pushed, including the overwriting push, so the production repository would receive the untested image as well. Forcing a new deployment makes tasks pull the current target of the mutable tag, which is exactly the behavior that caused the incident.

prompt: A health insurer's Lambda function named claims-sync reads a partner API token from an environment variable named PARTNER_API_TOKEN. A security review sets two requirements: the variable must be encrypted at rest under the customer managed key alias/claims-env, whose key policy the security team controls, and the token must also be encrypted client-side before it reaches the Lambda service, so that the function configuration returns only ciphertext for it. The team accepts a small code change.
Which configuration meets both requirements?
options: Use alias/claims-env for encryption at rest, encrypt the token with the encryption helpers and that key, decrypt it with KMS during init, and grant the role kms:Decrypt.
Use alias/claims-env for encryption at rest, and grant the execution role kms:Decrypt so that Lambda decrypts PARTNER_API_TOKEN before the handler starts.
Keep the default AWS managed key for encryption at rest, and enable the encryption helpers so that the console encrypts the token in transit with alias/claims-env.
Use alias/claims-env for encryption at rest, encrypt the token with the encryption helpers, and rely on Lambda to decrypt the value before the handler starts.
questions.explanation: Two separate settings are needed: choosing alias/claims-env as the at-rest key replaces the AWS managed key, and the encryption helpers encrypt the token client-side with that key, so the stored and returned value is ciphertext that the function decrypts itself with a KMS Decrypt call, cached once during initialization, which needs kms:Decrypt on the execution role. Selecting the customer managed key for encryption at rest alone satisfies the first requirement only, because Lambda decrypts at-rest values transparently and the configuration shows plaintext to anyone allowed to use the key. Keeping the AWS managed key fails the at-rest requirement outright. Lambda never decrypts helper-encrypted values on the function's behalf, so without decryption code the handler receives a base64 ciphertext string.

prompt: A freight company runs a Spring Boot service named route-planner on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer. On startup each task spends about 150 seconds loading routing graphs before its /health endpoint answers. The target group checks /health every 10 seconds with an unhealthy threshold of 3. During every deployment the new tasks are marked unhealthy after about 30 seconds, stopped by ECS and replaced, so the deployment never reaches a steady state. Tasks that do finish starting run without problems.
Which change lets new tasks finish starting while still replacing tasks that become unhealthy after startup?
options: Turn on the deployment circuit breaker with rollback so that the service returns to the last working task definition automatically.
Raise the minimum healthy percent of the service to 100 so that ECS keeps the old tasks running until the new tasks pass checks.
Set a health check grace period of 180 seconds on the ECS service and tune the target group health check interval and threshold.
Change the target group health check success codes to 200-499 so that a task that is still starting passes the health check.
questions.explanation: The service health check grace period tells the ECS scheduler to ignore load balancer health check results for that many seconds after a task starts, so 180 seconds covers the 150-second warm-up, and tuning the target group interval and unhealthy threshold keeps detection prompt but tolerant once the grace period ends, so tasks that fail later are still replaced. The circuit breaker would detect the repeated failures and roll back to the old revision, so the new version would never deploy. A minimum healthy percent of 100 keeps capacity up during the rollout, but the new tasks are still killed at 30 seconds and the deployment still never completes. Accepting 200-499 does not help a task that is not yet listening, and it would permanently hide real errors.

prompt: A web application stores user sessions in an Amazon DynamoDB table named UserSessions. Each item has an expiresAt attribute that holds the expiry time as a Unix epoch timestamp in seconds. A nightly AWS Lambda function scans the whole table and deletes expired items with BatchWriteItem, and its write consumption now accounts for a large share of the table's monthly bill.
Which change removes expired sessions at the lowest cost?
options: Enable Time to Live on the table with expiresAt as the TTL attribute so expired items are deleted in the background.
Add a global secondary index keyed on expiresAt and change the nightly function to Query it before deleting the items.
Write sessions into a new table every day and have a scheduled function delete the table that is more than a day old.
Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table with a retention period that matches the session lifetime so old items age out.
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Time to Live deletes items whose TTL attribute, a Number holding an epoch time in seconds, is in the past, and those background deletions consume no write capacity, so the nightly scan and its delete charges disappear. Deletion is not instant (it typically happens within a few days of expiry), so the application should keep ignoring sessions whose expiresAt has passed. A GSI on expiresAt makes finding expired items cheaper, but every delete is still a paid write and the index adds its own write cost. Rolling daily tables avoid per-item deletes but break sessions that span midnight and add table-management code. DynamoDB Streams keeps change records for a fixed 24 hours; it has no configurable retention and no effect on the items in the table.

prompt: A car-sharing startup has agreed on the contract for a REST API with GET /fleet/{vehicleId} and POST /bookings, including JSON response bodies and the 200, 201 and 404 status codes. The mobile team wants a shared HTTPS endpoint to build against this week, but the backend team will not start the Lambda functions for another month.
Which approach gives the mobile team a working endpoint that returns the agreed responses without writing or running any backend code?
options: Create placeholder Lambda functions that return hardcoded JSON for each route and attach them to the methods with Lambda proxy integration.
Configure each method with a mock integration whose integration responses return the agreed JSON bodies and status codes through mapping templates.
Enable API caching on the stage with a long time to live and prime the cache with sample responses so that requests never reach a backend.
Have each mobile developer run sam local start-api against a template that declares the routes so that the endpoints respond on each laptop.
questions.explanation: A mock integration makes API Gateway answer the request itself: the integration request mapping template selects a status code, and the integration responses return the agreed body and headers through mapping templates, so the deployed stage serves the contract over HTTPS with no backend at all and can later be switched to the real Lambda integrations. Placeholder Lambda functions work, but they are backend code that someone has to write, deploy and pay for, which the requirement rules out. API caching stores responses that a backend has already produced and cannot be primed with sample data, so every request would still need an integration. The sam local start-api command runs function code from the template locally, so with no functions written there is nothing to serve, and it would not be a shared endpoint anyway.

prompt: An online marketplace runs a Lambda function named checkout-api whose structured logs, written to the log group /aws/lambda/checkout-api, sometimes include customer email addresses and credit card numbers. Thirty support engineers query that log group daily with CloudWatch Logs Insights. Compliance requires these values to be hidden from everyone except a small security group, and the developers cannot change the application's logging code this quarter.
Which approach meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?
options: Add a subscription filter that streams the log group to a Lambda function, which redacts the values and writes the clean events to a second log group for the support team.
Create a data protection policy on the log group with managed data identifiers for email addresses and credit card numbers, and grant logs:Unmask only to security.
Enable Amazon Macie automated sensitive data discovery for the account, so that it detects and masks the values in the log group as new log events arrive.
Create metric filters that match email address and card number patterns in the log group, and alarm the security team whenever either filter matches an event.
questions.explanation: A CloudWatch Logs data protection policy detects the selected managed data identifiers as events are ingested and masks them at every egress point, including Logs Insights, metric filters and subscription filters, while principals granted logs:Unmask can still see the original values; it needs no code change. It applies only to events ingested after the policy is created, so older events stay as they were. A redaction pipeline built on a subscription filter is custom code to run and pay for, and the original log group still holds the unmasked values that support can query. Amazon Macie analyzes objects in Amazon S3, not CloudWatch Logs log groups, and it reports findings rather than masking data. Metric filters only count matches; every value stays fully visible.

prompt: A crowdfunding platform stores each pledge as an item in an Amazon DynamoDB table named Pledges. Campaign pages show a running total per campaign, which is kept in a second table named CampaignTotals. A scheduled AWS Lambda function scans Pledges every 15 minutes and rewrites every total, so totals lag by up to 15 minutes and the scan cost grows with every new pledge. Product managers want totals to update within a few seconds of each pledge.
Which approach meets the requirement with the least operational overhead?
options: Enable a DynamoDB stream on Pledges with the NEW_IMAGE view and add a Lambda trigger that adds each pledge to its campaign total.
Enable Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB on Pledges and have an Amazon Data Firehose stream deliver the records into CampaignTotals.
Enable CloudWatch Contributor Insights for DynamoDB on Pledges and read the per-campaign figures from its contributor reports.
Run the existing scan function every minute from an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule and keep rewriting every total.
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams captures every item change, and a Lambda event source mapping on the stream invokes the function within seconds, so it can apply an UpdateItem with an ADD expression to the matching campaign's total for each INSERT record. Stream records can be processed more than once after a retry, so the function should guard against double counting, for example with a conditional write keyed on the pledge ID. Amazon Data Firehose has no DynamoDB destination, so it cannot write into CampaignTotals. Contributor Insights reports the most frequently accessed and throttled keys, not sums of attribute values. Scanning every minute still lags by up to a minute and multiplies the already growing scan cost by fifteen.

prompt: A biotech company updates an AWS CloudFormation stack named lab-results-api to add a Lambda function and an IAM role and to change a global secondary index on an Amazon DynamoDB table. The update ends in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE. The stack events list now holds dozens of entries: the newest are rollback cleanup events, and several resources show UPDATE_FAILED with the status reason Resource update cancelled.
Where should the developer look to find the root cause of the failed update?
options: The status reason of the UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE event, which is the newest entry at the top of the stack events list.
The results of a drift detection run on the stack, which list each resource whose live configuration differs from the template.
The status reason of the earliest CREATE_FAILED or UPDATE_FAILED event that was recorded after the update operation began.
The status reason of the most recent UPDATE_FAILED event whose reason reads Resource update cancelled in the stack events.
questions.explanation: When one resource fails, CloudFormation cancels the operations still in flight and rolls back, so the cause is recorded on the first failure event of the update, and reading the stack events in time order to the earliest CREATE_FAILED or UPDATE_FAILED entry shows the real error, such as a permissions denial or an invalid property, in its status reason. The UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE event only reports that the rollback finished. Drift detection compares live resource configuration with the template; after a successful rollback the resources match the previous template, and drift says nothing about why the update failed. Events reading Resource update cancelled are consequences of the first failure, since CloudFormation stopped those updates because something else had already failed.

prompt: Five developers test a deployed Lambda function named payout-reconciler in a shared development account. Each developer keeps private JSON payload files on a laptop, the files have drifted apart, and bug reports keep turning out to be differences between payloads rather than defects. The team wants one set of named test events stored in the account, usable from the command line against the deployed function and visible in the Lambda console's test tab.
Which approach meets these requirements with the least custom tooling?
options: Save the payloads as shareable test events with sam remote test-event put, and have each developer run sam remote invoke with the --test-event-name option.
Save each payload as a private test event in the Lambda console under a common naming scheme, and have the developers invoke the function from the console.
Keep the payloads in the repository's events folder and have each developer run sam local invoke with the -e option against the function on a laptop.
Commit the payloads to the repository and have each developer pass the chosen file to aws lambda invoke with the --payload option against the function.
questions.explanation: Shareable test events are stored in the Amazon EventBridge schema registry and are visible to everyone in the account who has the schema permissions, so the same named events appear in the Lambda console's test tab, and the SAM CLI manages them with sam remote test-event and sends one to the deployed function with sam remote invoke and --test-event-name. Private test events in the console are visible only to the user who created them, so a shared naming scheme does not share them. Running sam local invoke tests a local container rather than the deployed function, with its real role, configuration and downstream resources. Committing files and calling aws lambda invoke does reach the deployed function, but the events live outside the account and never appear in the console's test tab.

prompt: A home-services marketplace stores free-text notes that support agents write after each customer call in an Amazon DynamoDB table named SupportNotes, where an analytics team mines them for recurring problems. The notes are in English, are up to 20 KB each, and pass through a Lambda function named notes-writer before they are stored. Agents often type customers' names, phone numbers, email addresses and street addresses into the notes, and privacy rules now require that this personal data be removed before the text is stored.
Which approach meets the requirement with the least development and maintenance effort?
options: Turn on DynamoDB encryption at rest with a customer managed KMS key for SupportNotes, so that the note text is protected before it is stored in the table.
Enable Amazon Macie for the account, so that it scans the SupportNotes table on a schedule and masks the personal data in each item after it is written.
Maintain regular expressions for names, phone numbers, email addresses and street addresses, and apply them in notes-writer to each note before the write.
Call Amazon Comprehend DetectPiiEntities from notes-writer, replace each returned offset range with its entity type, and then write the redacted text.
questions.explanation: DetectPiiEntities is a synchronous API that accepts up to 100 KB of English or Spanish text and returns each PII entity's type, confidence score and begin and end offsets, so notes-writer can swap each span for a label such as [PHONE] and store only redacted text, with the model maintained by AWS. ContainsPiiEntities returns only the entity labels present, which suits a fast yes-or-no check but not span replacement. Encryption at rest with a customer managed key protects the stored bytes, yet every reader with table access still sees the names and numbers in plaintext. Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in Amazon S3, not in DynamoDB items, and reports findings rather than masking anything. Hand-written regular expressions can catch email addresses but are poor at names and street addresses, and they become a pattern list the team must maintain forever.

prompt: An online bookstore keeps its catalog of about 2 million titles in an Amazon DynamoDB table named Books, which remains the system of record for orders and inventory. Shoppers need a search box that matches words anywhere in the title, author and description, tolerates typos, ranks results by relevance and filters by format and price. The current search runs a Scan with contains() filters, takes several seconds and consumes large amounts of read capacity.
Which approach provides this search capability while keeping DynamoDB as the system of record?
options: Add a global secondary index with title as its sort key and query it with a begins_with condition on the search text.
Put a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table so that the repeated Scan requests are cached.
Run PartiQL SELECT statements with a WHERE clause that uses contains() instead of calling the Scan API directly.
Replicate the table into Amazon OpenSearch Service, for example with the zero-ETL integration, and query its index.
questions.explanation: Amazon OpenSearch Service builds an inverted index with text analyzers, fuzzy matching, relevance scoring and aggregations for facets, which is what full-text search needs, and the DynamoDB zero-ETL integration, built on OpenSearch Ingestion, keeps the index in sync with the table without custom pipeline code while orders and inventory stay in DynamoDB. A begins_with key condition matches only a case-sensitive prefix of one sort key attribute, with no typo tolerance or ranking. DAX caches identical requests, but each distinct search is a new Scan, and a cached scan still has no relevance ranking or fuzzy matching. A PartiQL SELECT whose WHERE clause has no key condition is executed as a full table scan, so it costs the same as the Scan it replaces.
